newsitem.title: MEXICO: Clock ticks for new Mexican pension funds.
newsitem.headline: Clock ticks for new Mexican pension funds.

text.p: With time running out for banks to forge pension funds in Mexico, the banking group Serfin Wednesday joined forces with Citibank and a Chilean partner AFP Habitat to forge what they hope will be a powerhouse in the brand new industry.
"The time left to us is very short," said Juan Fernandez, head of the new pension fund management firm. "Every day of the week will be important."

Grupo Financiero Serfin, which owns Mexico's third-largest bank, has already made one failed attempt to seal a pension fund marriage with Spain's Banco Santander. But officials insisted the chemistry with its new partners was powerful.
It needs to be. Mexico plans to allow private-run pension funds to operate from Jan. 1, 1997, and Mexican banks have been scrambling to forge alliances to be ready in time.

The newly-formed fund does not yet have a name. Within the next 100 days, Fernandez said, it needs to hire some 6,000 employees including sales people and administrative staff. Because the industry is new, all of them have to be trained.

The initial investment, he said, would be at least $70 million, divided according to the stake each partner will have in the fund -- 51 percent for Serfin, 40 percent for Citibank and 9 percent for Habitat.

Some $5 million to $8 million of that investment will go toward the complex task of building computer software systems to process pension fund data for the 1 million to 1.5 million clients the fund hopes to attract.
President Ernesto Zedillo has not yet ratified final rules for the new fund business, though they are said to be ready. Officials said the delay was costing them precious time.
Also, players need to see how the rules work in practice before they can decide whether each new pension fund is playing on a level playing field.
"The rules as we've seen them are very competent. But implementation is the trick," Ricardo Zavala of AFP Habitat said after a signing ceremony to form the fund.

In Mexico, running pension funds has always been the preserve of the government. Mexican banks have little experience in canvassing for clients or offering them the sort of returns they will demand for a secure retirement.

Many have turned to Chilean partners who have 15 years of experience in handling pension accounts. Habitat, which is partly owned by Citibank in Chile, is one of the leading players in that market and Zavala said its experience will be crucial in ensuring the Mexican fund is ready in time.
The leading Chilean fund manager Provida has joined forces with the Spanish-Mexican bank BBV Probursa and a top Mexican insurer to form one rival, with an initial investment of $60 million.

Mexico's second largest bank Bancomer which already handles at least 36 percent of accounts in the government-run Retirement Savings System (SAR), has joined up with U.S. insurer Aetna Inc. and its Chilean subsidiary.
Serfin holds 12 percent of accounts in the SAR, and will need to canvass hard to gain the 17 percent market share that is the maximum allowed for each private pension fund.
